Data sourced from Dakota Marketplace, the global LP and GP intelligence platform trusted by thousands of investment professionals. Learn More | Book a Demo Advent International closed its eleventh flagship fund, GPE XI, at $27B on October 27, above its $26B target and the largest buyout fund to finish fundraising in 2026 so far (Business Wire, October 2026). It also lands after a quiet stretch for large buyout: large buyout fundraising fell to $28.0B in Q3 2026 from $76.2B in Q2, about 15% of the $183.9B raised for private equity in the quarter (Dakota Marketplace, Q3 2026). The next wave is already in market. At least $180B in flagship buyout targets sit across the funds below, and several aim for final closes in the first half of 2027. Whether they close on target will show how much institutional demand there is for buyout heading into the new year. In this article, we’ll cover the 10 largest flagship buyout fundraises to watch heading into 2027, where each one stands, what the pipeline signals for allocators, and what it means for investment firms raising outside the flagship group. Top 10 Buyout Fundraisers to Watch Heading Into 2027 How to Read This List The funds are ranked by target size, converted to USD. Each one is labeled by its current status (in pre-marketing, first close held, or nearing final close), and none of them has completed fundraising as of early November 2026. Targets and timelines come from firm announcements, pension documents, and press reports, so they may shift as each raise progresses. 1. CVC Capital Partners | Europe / Americas Fund X Status: Formal fundraising set to begin in January 2027, following roughly 18 months of pre-marketing Target: €26B (about $30.2B) in fee-paying commitments Predecessor: Europe / Americas IX closed at €27.3B (about $31.5B) in July 2023, 9% above its initial target Fund X is expected to follow the same strategy as its predecessor, which was 60% to 65% invested as of June. CVC’s last three Europe / Americas funds all closed above target, and the firm reports more than €56B in gross proceeds returned from the strategy since 2021. Source: CVC, September 2026. 2. EQT | EQT XI Status: First close held this summer at roughly 50% of target, with fundraising expected to continue throughout 2027 Target: €23B (about $27.0B), with a €24B (about $28.2B) hard cap Predecessor: EQT X, which kept raising for 12 to 18 months after its first close before reaching its hard cap EQT XI is set to be the firm’s largest fund. EQT has said its fundraising momentum is strong even as global industry fundraising volumes fell 13% over the past 12 months. Source: EQT Q3 announcement, October 2026. 3. Clayton, Dubilier & Rice | CD&R Fund XIII Status: About $20B raised within six months of launch, with a final close targeted for Q1 2027 Target: $26B, with a $28.5B hard cap Predecessor: Fund XII raised about $10B over a comparable period in 2023 before closing at roughly $26B Known LPs (Dakota Marketplace): Washington State Investment Board ($300M) Pennsylvania PSERS ($200M), Kansas Public Employees Retirement System ($135M) CD&R is raising at about twice the pace of its last fund, and several existing allocators are reportedly increasing their commitments. Source: Bloomberg via Private Equity Wire, October 2026. 4. Apollo Global Management | Apollo Investment Fund XI Status: Fundraising began in February 2026, with an initial close planned for later in 2026 and a final close in Q1 2027 Target: $22B to $25B Predecessor: Apollo Investment Fund X closed at $20B in August 2023 Known LPs: San Antonio Fire and Police Pension Fund and Louisiana State Employees’ Retirement System are reported to have committed Fund XI will pursue buyouts, corporate carve-outs, and deleveraging transactions, and could become Apollo’s largest private equity fund. Source: Buyouts, March 2026. 5. Permira | Permira IX Status: €9.4B (about $10.9B) first close Target: About €17B (about $19.7B) Predecessor: Permira VIII closed above its €15B target at €16.7B in March 2023 Known LPs (Dakota Marketplace): Washington State Investment Board ($400M), Minnesota State Board of Investment ($250M) Current and former Permira employees contributed about €1B of the first close, roughly 10% of capital raised so far. That’s one of the larger GP commitments in the market. Source: Private Equity News, September 2026. See who’s backing these funds. Dakota Marketplace tracks private equity commitments from public pension plan minutes, along with the allocators, consultants, and decision-makers behind them. See which allocators have committed to the largest buyout funds, and which are still deploying by booking a demo of Dakota Marketplace. 6. KKR | KKR Asian Fund V Status: In market since November 2025 Target: $15B Predecessor: KKR Asian Fund IV closed at $15B in 2021, the largest Asia-focused buyout fund raised at the time Known LPs: Louisiana State Employees’ Retirement System ($100M), approved on the recommendation of NEPC Asia-focused buyout has already drawn significant capital this year: EQT closed BPEA IX at $15.6B in April, and Bain Capital closed its sixth Asia fund at its $10.5B hard cap. Whether KKR reaches $15B will show how much room is left for Asia mega-funds. Source: Louisiana State Employees’ Retirement System board minutes, March 2026. 7. The Carlyle Group | Carlyle Partners IX Status: Launched in June 2026, with a first close targeted by year-end Target: About $15B Predecessor: Carlyle Partners VIII closed at $14.8B in August 2023, below its initial $22B target Carlyle is offering a 15 basis point management fee discount to allocators who commit before the first close. Ahead of the launch, it arranged an $8.5B structured financing that returned capital to existing investors and seeded more than $5B for the new fund. Source: Bloomberg, June 2026. 8. Apax Partners | Apax XII Status: First close expected by March 2027 Target: €12B (about $13.6B) Predecessor: Apax XI closed at more than $12B in March 2024, just short of its $13B target The target matches the predecessor’s final size rather than stepping up, a more measured approach than several funds on this list. Apax invests in technology, services, healthcare, and internet/consumer companies, primarily in North America and Western Europe. Source: Private Equity International, October 2026. 9. Bridgepoint | Bridgepoint Europe VIII Status: €6B (about $7.1B) first close in under six months, with a final close scheduled for 2027 Target: €7.5B (about $8.8B) Predecessor: Bridgepoint Europe VII closed at €7B in 2024, including co-investments Known LPs (Dakota Marketplace): Minnesota State Board of Investment ($200M), Washington State Investment Board ($200M) Bridgepoint invests in European middle-market businesses valued above €300m, across advanced industrials, business and financial services, healthcare, and technology. Source: Bloomberg, April 2026. 10. TJC | The Resolute Fund VII Status: Targeting a November 2026 close Target: $8.5B, with a $10.5B hard cap Predecessor: The Resolute Fund VI closed at $6.85B in January 2024, above its $6B hard cap Known LPs: Pennsylvania SERS ($150M), Pennsylvania PSERS ($150M), Illinois Firefighters’ Pension Investment Fund ($33M) Fund VII will target 25 to 28 North American middle-market and upper-middle-market companies with enterprise values of $100m to $2.5B. The target is roughly a 24% step-up from Fund VI’s final close. Source: Pennsylvania SERS staff memo, July 2026. What the Pipeline Signals Capital is concentrating in established franchises. Nearly every fund on this list is a flagship from a manager with a long record of closing at or above target, and several are raising faster than their predecessors. Slow distributions from older funds leave allocators with less capital to recycle, which favors re-ups with managers they already know. Flagship managers are moving into the middle market. Advent’s new mid-market fund has raised more than $3B for equity checks of $100M to $350M, and CVC closed its Europe-focused mid-market fund, CVC Catalyst III, at €3B in July, nearly double its initial target. That puts flagship brands in direct competition with independent mid-market firms for the same allocators. What to watch: Whether these raises close on target, whether a stronger IPO market speeds up distributions, and whether allocator demand broadens beyond the largest platforms in 2027. What It Means for Investment Firms Raising Outside the Flagship Group Plan for a longer fundraise. With capital concentrating in established franchises, managers outside that group should build extra time into their fundraising calendar. Offer co-investment capacity. Co-investment helps allocators keep deploying while lowering their blended fees, which keeps smaller managers relevant to plans that are prioritizing re-ups. Use peer participation as proof. Mid-sized public pensions tend to back the same funds, so each new commitment strengthens your case with the next plan. Track who is deploying right now. Public plan minutes show which allocators are approving new buyout commitments and which have paused, so outreach can focus on plans with capital to put to work.
